objectives: Explain why English changed differently in each country that adopted it.
Tell British, American and Australian English apart by everyday vocabulary.
Recognise the grammar that travelled with the language and settled differently.
Identify the pronunciation feature that separates American from British English.
Recognise Indian and Singapore English and the words they added to the language.
Ask a clarifying question instead of assuming a word has only one meaning.
Choose the register and variety that fit the conversation you are in.

sections.body:
English is used as an official language in more countries than any other language on earth, and it is spoken as a first language in several countries that are far apart and share almost no history. The result is that English has become a family of closely related varieties rather than a single standard form with foreign accents attached.

A **variety of English** is a set of shared habits: which words you use for things, how you build sentences, how you pronounce them. British English, American English, Australian English, Indian English and Singapore English are all English. Each is as correct as the others, and each is as easy for a local to understand as its own home variety.

Two ideas keep people confused. The first is that one variety is the original and the others are copies that drifted. That is not how it works. British English was itself a set of regional dialects before it was anything else, and it went on changing after it started travelling. The second idea is that an accent is a set of mistakes. Some non-standard forms are errors; most are simply different choices that became standard in one place and not elsewhere.

The important consequence is practical. When you meet an unfamiliar variety, you are not meeting bad English. You are meeting English that was taught in a different order, with different models of the language, in a different classroom. Understanding the variety is a matter of learning a second set of defaults, and that is far easier than learning a new language.
examples: That is not a mistake. It is the normal wording in this country.
Which variety do you use at home?
sections.heading: One language, many accents

sections.body:
English spread for three different reasons, and each reason left a different mark on the language.

The first is trade and piracy. Sailors from England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland spent centuries at sea and in port, mixing their dialects. The result is a mixed, practical, slightly roughened English that became the base for the varieties of the Americas, Australia and the Caribbean.

The second is settlement and administration. English speakers colonised large parts of the world from the seventeenth century onwards, and they brought their dialects with them. In India, English became the language of courts, universities and administration, and it is now one of the official languages of the country. In Singapore it became the working language of a port and of a government, next to Mandarin, Malay and Tamil.

The third is industry and technology. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, American English grew out of the largest English-speaking economy in the world, and it was carried around the world by film, music, publishing and software. This is why American vocabulary is now the default in most international organisations, and why most international business English sounds American rather than British.

The interesting point is that each of these layers added to the others. Indian English keeps British grammar from the colonial period and adds vocabulary from Hindi and other Indian languages. Singapore English is built on a British colonial grammar with vocabulary from Mandarin, Malay and Tamil, and a rhythm that owes much to the languages around it. Australian English carries the older British dialects and adds its own relaxed shortening. Nothing here is a copy of anything else; every variety is a mixture that grew up in its own place.
examples: English came here first through trade, then through schools and courts.
The rhythm of the language comes from the languages spoken around it.
sections.heading: Why the language split up

sections.body:
Vocabulary is the quickest way to place an English speaker, and the easiest part of a variety to learn. You need only a short list to hold an ordinary conversation.

**British and American English** differ most in everyday nouns. British English says **lift** where American English says **elevator**, **petrol** where American English says **gas**, **rubbish** where American English says **trash**, **jumper** where American English says **sweater**, **trainers** where American English says **sneakers**, **flat** where American English says **apartment**, **queue** where American English says **line**, **holiday** where American English says **vacation**. Words for institutions differ too: British English says **school**, American English says **elementary school** and **high school**. And spelling shows it plainly: **colour**, **centre**, **organise**, **travelling** against **color**, **center**, **organize**, **traveling**.

**Australian English** keeps many British words and shortens them. An Australian says **arvo** for the afternoon, **brekkie** for breakfast, **servo** for a petrol station, **footpath** for the pavement, **bathers** for swimwear, **mozzies** for mosquitoes, and **no worries** for a great many situations. Australian English also tends to prefer **take a look** where British English often says **have a look**.

**Indian English** adds words from Indian languages and from the working world of the British Raj. You may hear **chai** for tea, **dacoit** for a bandit, **lunch** for a light meal, **vegetable** in the sense of a large dish of curried vegetables, **prepone** for the opposite of postpone, and **revert** used for simply answering. Indian English also keeps British institutional vocabulary intact: **president** for the head of an institution, **principal** for the head of a school, and the habit of calling a woman **madam**.

**Singapore English** is marked by words borrowed from Mandarin and Malay. A **kopitiam** is a coffee shop, **canh** is soup, **char kway teow** is a noodle dish, **shiok** means very or extremely, and **lah** and **lor** add the particular cadence at the end of a sentence. In formal Singapore English you also hear **minimise** instead of **minimize**, **organisation** rather than **organization**, and **practise** as a noun and **practice** as a verb.

Two rules make this manageable. First, never assume a word has one global meaning: a **lift** in London is a device that carries you; in the rest of the world it is the journey up. Second, when a word is unfamiliar, ask for the local word rather than guessing from the American one, because the American word is often the one that will not be understood locally.
examples: Could you say that another way? I know the American word but not the local one.
Is that a lift, or are you going up the stairs?
sections.heading: Vocabulary: the same thing, a different word

sections.body:
These are the terms you need to talk about English itself, and to read an article or a dictionary note about it.

A **variety** is a form of a language used by a particular group in a particular place. An **accent** is how the sounds of a language are pronounced by a speaker. **Dialect** is a variety tied to a region, a class or a social group. **Idiolect** is the individual version: the habits of one particular speaker.

**Rhoticity** is the naming feature that says whether a language pronounces the r sound at the end of a word. British, Australian, Indian and Singapore English are mostly **non-rhotic**, so *car* sounds like *cah*. American English is **rhotic**, so the r is pronounced: *car*. This is the clearest single sound difference between the two.

**Anglicism** is a word borrowed from English into another language. **Loanword** is the general term for any word taken from another language. A **lingua franca** is a shared language used between people who have different first languages. **Register** is the level of formality a speaker chooses: the same person says *Could you pass the salt* at dinner and *Pass the salt* to a colleague.

**Code-switching** is moving between two languages, or between two varieties of one language, inside a single conversation. **Spanglish** and **Hinglish** are the names usually given to the mixes of Spanish and English, and of Hindi and English. **Standardisation** is the process a variety goes through when it is taught, written down and fixed by schools, broadcasters and dictionaries. **Anglicisation** is the process by which a language replaces its own words with English ones.

**Spelling reform** is the deliberate redesign of a spelling system, and **standard English** is the form taught in schools and used in official writing, which is only one of the varieties that exist.
examples: That is a different register, not a different language.
English is the lingua franca of this meeting.
sections.heading: The words that describe the variety

terms.example: Singapore English is a variety of English, not a broken version of it.
terms.gloss: A form of English used by a particular group in a particular place, with its own vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation.

terms.example: He has a strong Glasgow accent but standard vocabulary.
terms.gloss: The way the sounds of a language are pronounced by a speaker, independent of which words they use.

terms.example: The difference between *car* and *cah* is rhoticity.
terms.gloss: Whether a speaker pronounces the r sound at the end of a word. American English is rhotic; British English is not.

terms.example: Switching register, he changed *Could you pass the salt* to *Pass the salt*.
terms.gloss: The level of formality a speaker chooses for a situation, from casual to formal.

terms.example: Code-switching between English and Tamil is normal in Chennai offices.
terms.gloss: Moving between two languages, or two varieties of one language, inside a single conversation.

terms.example: English works as the lingua franca, so nobody has to learn three languages for one meeting.
terms.gloss: A shared language used between people whose first languages differ. English is the most common one in international business.

terms.example: Every email you write becomes part of your idiolect.
terms.gloss: The individual version of a language: one speaker's own habits of words and grammar.

sections.body:
Vocabulary is the loudest difference, but grammar changes too, and grammar changes are what make you sound foreign.

**Have got** is the everyday form in British, Irish, Australian, Indian and Singapore English. British speakers say *I have got a car*; American speakers say *I have a car*, and using *have got* in New York is instantly noticeable. In American English the past of *get* is **gotten**, so *I've gotten a lot of work*, while British English usually keeps **got**.

The phrasal verb is the biggest battleground. British English uses *have a look*, *have a go*, *have a wash*. American English prefers *take a look*, *give it a go*, *give it a wash*. Indian English tends toward the British pattern, and Singapore English uses both freely, often with *have a look* alongside *take a look*.

**Question tags** behave differently too. British English uses them more, and more widely: *You're coming, aren't you?* In American English the tag is often *right?*, dropped onto the end of any statement. Indian English uses a lot of *isn't it*, *na?* and *yes?*, which reflects other Indian languages as much as English.

**Tenses and modals** shift in use more than in form. British English may say *I might have* where American English says *I might*, and American English often marks the present perfect with *already* and *just* where British English leaves them out. British English uses *shall* for offers and suggestions (*Shall we go?*) where American English normally uses *will* or *do you want to*.

**Prepositions** wander. British English says *at* a festival where American English says *at* too, but *in hospital* versus *in the hospital*, *at university* versus *at college*, and *different from* versus *different than* are reliable signs.

None of this is correct or incorrect in itself. Each form is standard in the place that uses it, and the danger is only in thinking your own form is the only one.
examples: I have got an appointment, so I cannot stay long.
Shall we order now, or would you rather look at the menu?
sections.heading: Grammar that travelled and settled differently

sections.body:
Sound is the last thing to learn and the first thing a listener notices, because speech is heard long before it is read.

The British and American divide is mostly about the letter r and a small set of vowel changes. American English pronounces the r in *car*, *farm* and *work*. British English does not, and the same words sound like *cah*, *fahm* and *wurk*. American English tends to pronounce the r in *bird* and *work* where British English does not. Beyond that, British English has a set of vowel shifts, so *about* and *out* reach further back in the mouth, and the stressed first syllable of a word is often longer than in American English.

Australian English keeps the non-rhotic r and adds its own vowel movement, so *dance* and *ask* stretch into a long vowel, and the stress tends to fall on the first syllable of a two-syllable word: *ˈfarmer* rather than *farˈmer*.

Indian English and Singapore English usually keep British pronunciation for the r but add rhythm from other languages. Singapore English, for example, tends to give final consonants more emphasis and to clip them harder, and it stresses the last syllable of many words where British English stresses an earlier one.

Stress is worth more attention than it first appears. If you stress the wrong syllable, the word may not be understood at all. A two-syllable noun that is stressed on the first syllable stays a noun: **ˈteacup**. Stress it on the second and it becomes a verb: **to teacup**, meaning to serve tea to someone.

The practical method is not to imitate an accent. It is to make your own words easier to catch: keep the vowel sounds clear, place the stress where your listener expects, and slow down slightly when a word carries the meaning of the sentence.
examples: Sorry, could you repeat that? I did not catch the last word.
It is a ˈteacup, not a place to keep tea.
sections.heading: Pronunciation and stress: the hardest layer

sections.body:
Here are ordinary sentences written the way people actually write them in five places. Use them as models, not as trivia.

In **British English**: *Sorry, could you let me know when the train leaves?* *I have got a meeting at half past three.* *Shall we grab a coffee?* *The bill, please.* *That's a bit of a shame.*

In **American English**: *Sorry, could you let me know when the train leaves?* *I have a meeting at three thirty.* *Want to grab a coffee?* *Check, please.* *That's a shame.*

In **Australian English**: *Sorry, could you let me know when the train leaves?* *I've got a meeting at three thirty.* *Shall we grab a coffee?* *The cheque, please.* *No worries.* *Not bad.*

In **Indian English**: *Sorry, could you let me know when the train leaves?* *I have got a meeting at half past three, madam.* *Shall we grab a coffee?* *The bill, please.* *Only yesterday.* *What is your good name?*

In **Singapore English**: *Sorry, could you let me know when the train leaves?* *I got a meeting at three thirty.* *Shall we grab a coffee?* *The bill, please.* *Can, can.* *Very steady, lah.*

Notice what is common to all five: the sentence structure is nearly identical, and only a few words change. That is the point. A listener who knows these few words can follow you in any of the five varieties, and you can switch to match them.

If you are unsure which variety to use, use the one your listener uses. People do not mind hearing British English in Singapore; they mind being talked to in a language they cannot follow.
examples: No worries, we can do it tomorrow.
Only yesterday, the whole system went down.
sections.heading: Sentences you can copy in each variety

sections.body:
You do not need to become a linguist to follow English you were not taught. Work through this in order, and the comprehension problem shrinks fast.

The order matters because vocabulary gives you the meaning immediately, while pronunciation is the layer that only slows you down. Get the meaning first and you can survive the sound.
examples: How do you say that here? I only know the American word.
Could you write that down for me? I want to check it later.
sections.heading: How to follow an unfamiliar variety
steps: Listen for the words you know from the local news, and write down the ones you did not know.
Ask what a word means in the local wording, not the American one.
Check the grammar by reading one local novel or one local news site for ten minutes.
Note the two or three phrasal verbs they use most, and use those yourself.
Copy one sentence you liked, exactly as it was said.
Switch to their variety for the length of one conversation, then decide what feels comfortable.

sections.body: A **mistake** is a form that no community of English speakers uses and that breaks a rule of the language, such as *I am having* used to mean *I am eating* in a formal register, or a missing article before a countable noun. A **variety** is a form that a whole community uses regularly, such as *I have got a car*, *gotten*, *different than*, or ending a sentence with *isn't it?*. Teachers sometimes correct a variety as a mistake, which is a habit of their training rather than a rule of the language. The practical test is simple: if millions of people in one city say it every day without anyone complaining, it is a variety, not an error.
sections.heading: What is a mistake and what is only a variety

sections.body:
Nobody speaks one English everywhere. People code-switch all the time, and a fluent bilingual meeting is a mixture of two or three varieties in a single hour.

You choose a variety for practical reasons. If you are writing to a customer in the United States, use American vocabulary, because their software, their support pages and their colleagues use it. If you are applying for a job in London, British English is the safer default. If you are doing business in Chennai or Singapore, the local variety is the most respectful choice and often the one that builds trust fastest.

Switching mid-conversation is normal and not something to apologise for. A speaker in Singapore may say *Can, can* inside an otherwise standard British sentence, and nobody treats it as an error. The rule that matters is not about mixing; it is about making yourself understood.

There is also a social point. The way English is used in each country carries the history of who used it there and in what position. Where English was the language of administration, it still sounds administrative. Where it grew up in the playground and on the street, it sounds relaxed. When you copy the local variety, you are not only copying the words; you are acknowledging that the language grew up there too.
examples: I will use the local wording here, so it lands properly with the customer.
She mixes two varieties in one meeting and it sounds completely natural.
sections.heading: Choosing a variety and switching between them

item.summary: English is one language with many accents, and most of the differences you meet are regular rather than wrong. After reading this you can recognise British, American, Australian, Indian and Singapore English by their vocabulary and grammar, understand why the differences exist, and choose the variety that fits your listener.
item.title: Why English Is Different Around the World
